newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seen hiking liquor tax to satisfy EU.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seen hiking liquor tax to satisfy EU.

text.p: South Korea is expected to raise its tax on a popular traditional liquor to head off a fight with Europe over the wide gap between tax rates on domestic and imported liquors, analysts said on Wednesday.
"A concession from the South Korean government appears unavoidable since the European Union has taken the issue to the WTO," said Han Young-hye, an analyst at ING-Baring Securities.

The EU filed an action with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in April, requesting consultations over what it said was South Korea's discriminatory tax regime on liquors. The consultations are set to start in Geneva on May 29.
South Korea currently levies a 35 percent tax on the local soju liquor and a 100 percent tax on whisky.
Han said the Korean government would raise the soju tax, probably to about 70 percent, rather than lower its whisky tax because it would not want to reduce tax revenues.
Sung Myung-jae, research fellow at the Korea Institute of Public Finance, said South Korea's tax rate on soju was too low.
"The whisky tax rate should be kept at a minimum of 100 percent but the soju tax rate should be raised to 62.5 percent," Sung said.
A Trade Ministry official said the South Korean government would not discuss its response to the EU prior to the talks.
Soju producers were outraged at the thought of a tax hike.
"You can't put soju and whisky in the same category," said an official at the Korea Alcohol and Liquor Association. "Their prices, quality and consumer groups are very different."

A soju producer group argued that soju was cheaper, had an alcohol strength of 25 percent and targeted lower income groups, while whisky was more expensive, had an alcohol content of 40 percent and was favoured by higher income consumers.
"If the soju tax rate is increased, it would put a heavy burden on local soju companies," the statement said.
Analysts said soju sales would decline if the tax increased.
Koreans drank about 774 million litres of soju last year, according to the liquor association, which said consumption had been flat in recent years.
The EU delegation in Seoul said it was seeking a balance between soju and whisky taxes rather than a specific rate.

"It is for any nation to decide how much they want to tax liquor. But there has to be no discrimination against imported liquor in terms of taxation," said a senior official of the EU delegation in Seoul, who declined to be identified.
The EU official said the delegation hoped to settle the issue during the consultations. If not, the next step under WTO rules would be bringing the issue to a dispute-resolution panel.
"We will, of course, use that opportunity because the EU brought Japan to a panel and the panel ruled in our favour," he said.
"There is no dramatic difference between the liquor taxation systems in Korea and Japan. Therefore, we feel that we have a good chance of winning the case."
Japan has moved to narrow the tax-rate gap between domestic liquors and imported whiskys to less than three percent after the WTO ruled against Tokyo in a similar complaint filed by the EU last year.
